newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine Central Bank refutes Thai comparison.
newsitem.headline: Philippine Central Bank refutes Thai comparison.

text.p: Philippine Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said on Tuesday that the country's financial sector remained sound and was not about to suffer the same fate as Thailand.

In a seven-page statement, Singson said critical indicators showed Philippine banks have not overextended their credits, including the real estate sector, and loan quality has not deteriorated as a result.
"More careful analyses of the market situation of each country would reveal fundamental differences in what first appear to be similar situations," Singson said.
Thailand's financial sector slumped into chaos recently due to rising bad debts especially from property loans which were hit by collapsing prices.

While bank credit grew by 51.9 percent in 1996, Singson said the 59.9 percent credit-to-gross national product ratio was still lower than in other Asian countries. Thailand's ratio was at 93 percent in 1994.
"For our level of development, therefore, the level of economic activity financed through credit is still way below prudent ceilings," Singson said.
Despite more loans, non-performing assets were only 3.3 percent of total loans in 1996, down from 4.2 percent in 1994.
Past due loans declined to 3.8 percent in 1996 from 4.7 percent in 1994. Singson added that banks have provided loss reserves covering 42 percent of the total past due loans.
The Philippine banking sector's capital adequacy ratio is 17 percent almost double that of Thailand's 9.6 percent and Korea's 9.0 percent, Singson added.
He said that as a percentage of gross domestic product, the exposure of Philippine banks to the real estate sector was only 3.6 percent, lower than Thailand's 21 percent.
As a percentage of the total loans, exposure to the property sector comprised only 10.9 percent.
"The bulk of bank credits continued to be absorbed by the productive sectors of the economy, namely manufacturing, which accounted for the largest share of 32.0 percent of total loans."
Singson also said 52 percent of the banks' foreign exchange loans were owed to residents as compared with only one percent in Thailand, adding that most of the loans are short-term loans.

In terms of foreign currency deposits, 86 percent of the deposit liabilities were from residents, many of whom were exporters. "Thus, the Philippine deposit system is very much less subject to any possible capital flight," it added.
Singson reiterated the peso, unlike the Thailand baht, is purely market driven and not artificially overvalued.

"If for any reason, the exchange rate is considered by the financial markets to be overvalued and the authorities refuse to devalue their currency, then heavy capital outflows will take place. That such outflows are not occurring is another indication that the prevailing exchange rate reflects economic fundamentals," he said.
A widening trade deficit has also been tagged as possible source of shock in the future.
He said the merchandise trade deficit was too narrow a measure of international transactions since exports have shifted away from goods and more into services.
